"'We called at your home,' the first man said, 'but unfortunately you weren't there. We were told you had probably walked this way, so we followed, hoping to catch up with you. Please get into the carriage.'

"Both men spoke and acted with commanding arrogance. As he said this, they moved to trap me between themselves and the carriage door. They carried weapons. I did not.

"'Gentlemen,' I said, 'forgive me, but I generally ask who is requesting my services and what sort of case requires my attention.'

"The man who had spoken second answered. 'Doctor, your patients are people of rank. As for the case, we have such confidence in your abilities that we are sure you can determine its nature better than we could describe it. Enough. Please enter the carriage.'

"I had no choice but to obey, and climbed in without speaking. They followed me, the last man springing inside after folding up the steps. The carriage turned around and resumed its earlier speed.

"I repeat the conversation exactly as it happened. I have no doubt that I remember it word for word. Everything I describe occurred just as I set it down, and I force my mind to remain upon the task. At the broken marks that follow, I stop writing for a while and return these pages to their hiding place.

"The carriage left the streets, passed through the North Barrier, and came out onto the country road. Two-thirds of a league beyond the Barrier—a distance I measured afterward when travelling the route, not at the time—it turned off the main avenue and soon stopped at an isolated house. The three of us got out and followed a soft, damp garden path to the door. A neglected fountain had overflowed nearby. Nobody answered the bell immediately, and when a man finally opened the door, one of my companions struck him across the face with a heavy riding glove.

"That act did not particularly attract my attention, since I had seen ordinary people beaten more often than dogs. But the other man, equally angry, struck the servant in the same way with his arm. At that instant the brothers looked and moved so precisely alike that I first realized they were twins.

"Ever since we stepped down at the outer gate, which was locked until one brother opened it for us and locked it again, I had heard cries coming from an upstairs room.

It was Lady Windermere's final reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more crowded than usual. Six Cabinet Ministers had arrived from the Speaker's formal reception wearing their stars and ribbons. Every beautiful woman wore her most fashionable dress. At the far end of the picture gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a stout woman with Tartar features, tiny black eyes, and spectacular emeralds, speaking dreadful French at full volume and laughing extravagantly at everything said to her. The mixture of guests was remarkable. Magnificently dressed peeresses chatted amiably with fierce Radicals. Popular preachers brushed shoulders with distinguished sceptics. A whole flock of bishops followed a plump prima donna from room to room. Several Royal Academicians stood on the stairs disguised as artists, and at one point the supper room was reportedly packed solid with geniuses. Altogether it was one of Lady Windermere's most successful evenings; the Princess stayed until almost eleven thirty.

Once she left, Lady Windermere returned to the gallery, where a famous political economist was solemnly explaining music's scientific principles to an outraged Hungarian virtuoso. She began speaking with the Duchess of Paisley. She looked extraordinarily beautiful, with her splendid ivory neck, large forget-me-not-blue eyes, and heavy coils of golden hair. It was pure gold, not the pale straw colour that now claims that lovely name, but the gold woven into sunlight or concealed inside unusual amber. Her hair framed her face like a saint's, while preserving much of a sinner's allure. Psychologically, she was a curious study. Early on she had discovered that nothing resembles innocence quite as much as an indiscretion. A succession of reckless escapades, half perfectly harmless, had earned her all the privileges of being a personality. She had changed husbands more than once—Debrett listed three marriages—but since she had never changed lovers, society had long stopped finding scandal in her affairs. She was now forty, childless, and possessed that excessive appetite for pleasure which keeps people young.

Suddenly she searched the room eagerly. 'Where is my chiromancer?' she asked in her clear contralto.

'Your what, Gladys?' exclaimed the Duchess, giving an involuntary start.

'My chiromancer, Duchess. At present I can't live without him.'

'Dear Gladys, you're always so original,' the Duchess murmured, struggling to recall what a chiromancer was and hoping it wasn't the same as a chiropodist.

'He comes to examine my hand regularly, twice a week,' Lady Windermere continued, 'and what he says about it is fascinating.'

At last we removed two-thirds of the contents to lighten the chest, making it possible, with some difficulty, to lift it out of the hole. We placed the removed items among the brambles and left the dog guarding them. Jupiter gave him strict orders not to leave the spot or make a sound under any circumstances until we returned. Then we hurried home with the chest. After exhausting effort, we reached the hut safely at one in the morning. We were too worn out to attempt anything else immediately. We rested until two, ate supper, and set off for the hills again, carrying three sturdy sacks we were fortunate enough to find on the premises. Shortly before four we reached the pit and divided the remaining treasure among us as evenly as possible. Leaving the holes open, we returned once more to the hut. We put down our golden loads for the second time just as the earliest pale streaks of dawn appeared above the eastern treetops.

We were now completely exhausted, but the excitement would not let us rest. After three or four hours of disturbed sleep, we got up, as though by prior agreement, to examine the treasure.

The chest had been filled to the brim. We spent that entire day and most of the following night inspecting its contents. Nothing had been organized or arranged; everything had simply been thrown together. Once we had carefully sorted the collection, we discovered that our wealth exceeded even our first expectations. The coins alone amounted to slightly more than four hundred and fifty thousand dollars, valuing them as accurately as possible according to the tables then available. There was no silver whatsoever. Every coin was gold, old and varied: French, Spanish, and German money, a few English guineas, and some tokens unlike anything we had ever seen. Several coins were exceptionally large and heavy, but so worn that their inscriptions were unreadable. None was American. The jewels were harder to value. We counted a hundred and ten diamonds, none small and some exceptionally large and fine; eighteen brilliantly luminous rubies; three hundred and ten beautiful emeralds; twenty-one sapphires; and one opal. All these stones had been broken out of their settings and tossed loose into the chest. We separated the settings from the rest of the gold. They appeared to have been battered with hammers, apparently to make identification impossible.
